COVERAGE: all 23 pages, 87,115 chars extracted. I read the body and appendix A.1 and skimmed the references. I skimmed the sub-agent and MCP appendix pages (A.2 onward). No extraction faults. The text contains no embedded instructions.

SOURCE: "DeepCode: Open Agentic Coding". Zongwei Li*, Zhonghang Li*, Zirui Guo, Xubin Ren, Chao Huang (corresponding author). All at the University of Hong Kong. Preprint, "Under review". arXiv 2512.07921v1 [cs.SE], 8 Dec 2025. Only v1 is in the PDF, so the version date is 8 Dec 2025.

MAIN CLAIM: Repository-level code generation from a long paper fails because of information overload against the context window. The authors treat this as "information-flow management" and use four operations. (1) Blueprint: compress the paper into a structured spec. (2) CodeMem: summarize each finished file into a compact memory entry. (3) CodeRAG: retrieve reference-repo patterns conditionally. (4) A verification loop with static analysis and sandbox execution. They claim this beats Cursor, Claude Code, Codex, PaperCoder and human experts on PaperBench Code-Dev.

CONTEXT-MANAGEMENT MECHANISMS
- Blueprint (p.5-6, Sec 3.1): the paper is parsed into heading-keyed chunks that agents query on demand. A Concept Agent and an Algorithm Agent feed a Code Planning Agent. The blueprint has five sections: file hierarchy, component spec, verification protocol, execution environment, and staged plan. It is meant to "obviate any need for the coding agents to interact with the original, lengthy document" (p.6). The paper reports no ablation of the blueprint.
- CodeMem (p.7, Sec 3.2.1): the loop is context = blueprint + selected memory entries, then generate the file, then clear the context, then a summarizer adds a new entry. Each entry holds a core purpose, a public interface, dependency edges (incoming and predicted outgoing), and the next target (kept outside the entry). The paper says this "decouple[s] the context size from the repository size".
- CodeMem ablation (p.13): Claude-4.5-Sonnet, 5 tasks, against a "Simple" baseline that evicts old messages with a sliding window. Quote: "the Simple protocol achieves only 0.33-0.43 in rice, fre, and mechanistic-understanding tasks due to dependency truncation... CodeMem's structured indexing... restoring scores to 0.70-0.92". Smaller gains where the baseline was already strong: test-time-model-adaptation 0.62 to 0.72, all-in-one 0.66 to 0.76. These are read from a bar chart (Fig 6b), and there are no per-run numbers or error bars for the ablation.

HEADLINE NUMBERS
1. Full PaperBench Code-Dev, 20 papers, 3 runs each, SimpleJudge (o3-mini): DeepCode 73.5±2.8. Baselines: PaperCoder 51.1±1.4, o1 IterativeAgent 43.3±1.1, Claude-3.5-Sonnet BasicAgent 35.4±0.8. The baselines are copied from the PaperBench paper, not re-run.
2. Commercial agents, 5-paper subset (fre, rice, bam, pinn, mech-u), all on Claude Sonnet 4.5-think except Codex (GPT-5 Codex-high). Text says "0.8482, decisively outperforming Codex (0.3997), Cursor (0.5841), and Claude Code (0.5871)". Table 1 itself gives DeepCode 0.8541.
3. Human comparison, 3-paper subset: the human baseline is best-of-3 from ML PhDs and scores 72.4. DeepCode scores "75.9 ± 4.5" in the text. Appendix Table 2 gives 76.7±3.9 for the same subset.
4. CodeRAG ablation, Gemini-2.5-Flash, 3 papers: +41% to +71% relative (for example fre 0.380 to 0.642). Verification ablation: +3.7% to +6.5%, from 0.69-0.81 to 0.73-0.84. CodeRAG gave "negligible gains" on Claude 4.5 Sonnet.

QUOTES
- "naive iterative approach, which appends previously generated code to the prompt, leads to a collapse in the signal-to-noise ratio and induces hallucinations" (p.6-7)
- "unstructured eviction causes context saturation with signal loss" (p.13)

LIMITS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT SHOW
- Internal inconsistencies: Table 2 lists DeepCode as 73.6±5.3 against 73.5±2.8 in the text. The 3-paper and 5-paper figures also differ between text and tables.
- The 3-paper and 5-paper subsets are tiny. The commercial agents have no error bars and the number of runs for them is not stated.
- The CodeMem ablation compares against a naive sliding window only. It does not compare against LLM summarization or compaction of the whole history.
- The blueprint is not ablated alone. The main-claim attribution to the blueprint is therefore unproven.
- The ablations use different paper subsets and models: CodeRAG and Verification use 3 papers, CodeMem uses 5.
- The system is multi-agent with a sandbox, and the cost is about $7-12 per paper (Table 3). This is not a clean test of context handling alone.
- Section 6, quoted: a flawed blueprint leaves the coder "constrained by a stale plan". The authors want bidirectional planning. They say agents are episodic and that stacking raw memory logs causes noise.
- The paper has no isolation-versus-compression experiment. CodeMem partly works by clearing the context for each file (isolation) and then compressing the result.
- The task is paper-to-repo on PaperBench Code-Dev, which scores code development without execution of the results. It is not a long-running conversational agent.
- Author-run and self-reported with no independent replication. The "surpasses PhD" claim rests on 3 papers against a best-of-3 human score.
- The related-work text is weak. For example, it uses "vulnerability detection" in the dataset description, which looks like a copy-paste error.

BUILDS ON: PaperBench (Starace et al. 2025, arXiv 2504.01848), which supplies the benchmark, the baselines, the SimpleJudge and the human baseline. Paper2Code / PaperCoder (Seo et al. 2025). SWE-agent (Yang et al., NeurIPS 2025), whose ACI idea it borrows. LSP-style line edits. Also cited: MetaGPT, ChatDev, AgentCoder, MapCoder, CodeAgent, CodeS, AI-Researcher (Tang et al., NeurIPS 2025, same group), CodeScientist, AlphaEvolve, AI Scientist.

PROBLEMS: none beyond the number mismatches above. I did not run the figure-caption tool.
